name: Wei Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, AI firms or political parties. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and run a drilling rig at a large open mine, making the holes used to break up the rock. I've a two-year technical diploma and lead our small rig crew; I like getting a straight hole in difficult ground, and I don't like fixing somebody else's rushed checks. This mine pays less than many, with few other mining employers close by. My partner checks invoices at a wholesaler, we've two children at school and a mortgage, and savings cover less than a month. I sometimes use AI to organise my own notes after somebody has shown me a useful example, but I don't put drilling instructions into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a little less paperwork would be welcome. I wouldn't call it a new age for drilling if we're still handling the same rig and checking the same ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our oldest child needs dental work, and that's already using money I wanted to keep for emergencies. I'm not expecting AI to remove my job in this picture. I am worried a lost week of overtime would leave us choosing which payment to delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the rig shifts and the checks we do before each move. This weekend my partner and I will write a payment calendar for the dental bill and the mortgage. We'll set aside 15 a week from fewer bought coffees through the first year, rather than assume ordinary work means spare money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, though I can put the worry into numbers. When I know which bill lands first, I stop imagining every bill arriving together. The problem is the small balance, not whether I can do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first timing problem on that calendar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dental payment comes two days before my wages. I'd ask the clinic whether we could move that date, without changing the total. It's an awkward call, but easier than pretending the account will stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone surprised that a senior operator is worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a colleague that doing well at work and having cash at home aren't the same. Our mortgage is based on both wages arriving. My drilling record is tidy, but the dental bill doesn't read my drilling record.

say: I welcome **less paperwork** without pretending a small software improvement changes the physical work of drilling.
I still expect **rig checks** and careful ground work to matter as much as before.
think: I worry that **lost overtime** would collide with the dental bill and mortgage despite my secure-looking work record.
I need **both wages** to arrive on time because our savings cover less than a month.
do: Keep the usual **rig shifts** and complete checks before moving equipment to the next hole.
Write a **payment calendar** and set aside 15 weekly by reducing bought coffees through the first year.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but putting dates against bills stops every cost becoming one imagined emergency.
S0.quote: My drilling record is tidy, but the dental bill doesn't read my drilling record.
fieldNote: The current **dental expense** explains anxiety in a mild scenario without inventing immediate automation of a hands-on job.
He uses **figures and dates** to manage worry, showing control without confusing a clear plan with an adequate financial cushion.

steps.text: Keep rig shifts and finish the checks before each equipment move
Set aside 15 weekly by reducing bought coffees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let a proven system help with paperwork, but keep the rig checks with us. I'd ask whoever tested it what errors they found, not just how many minutes they saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first risk at home might be my partner's invoice work, not my drilling. Checking and buying are right there in the picture you read. My own shifts still look needed, but if the wholesaler cuts hours our mortgage gets tighter immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask my partner to find out what invoice work the employer actually plans to automate. At the mine I'll take a paid demonstration of the planning tool after another rig crew has tried it. In the first year we'll keep saving 15 weekly and cancel our short holiday if either rota loses hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because the household has two different exposures, and one is easy to overlook. My job looking steady doesn't pay the other half of the bills. I want evidence before making big decisions, not reassurance based on my boots being muddy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What question would you suggest your partner asks at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask how many paid hours are planned next quarter and whether checking exceptions still needs staff. My partner would ask directly rather than rely on a colleague's rumour. We could budget with an answer, even an unwelcome one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household commitment would you change if hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the holiday booking first, before borrowing for ordinary bills. The children would be disappointed, and I'd explain that we were keeping the house payment safe. My muddy boots don't protect my partner's invoice wage.

say: I want **error evidence** from a trial before trusting a planning system with new responsibilities.
I would accept **paperwork help** while keeping the physical rig checks with trained operators.
think: I see **invoice work** as an earlier household exposure than my own hands-on drilling shifts.
I know **two wages** carry the mortgage, so my job alone cannot make the household safe.
do: Ask my partner to establish **planned invoice hours** and the wholesaler's actual automation plans.
Attend a **paid demonstration** after a rig crew trial and cancel the short holiday if either rota shrinks.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the combined household risk and want evidence before making large changes.
S1.quote: My muddy boots don't protect my partner's invoice wage.
fieldNote: He recognises **household exposure** beyond the miner archetype, linking the card's checking tasks to his partner's stated job.
His response combines **cautious learning** with a conditional spending cut, rather than assuming curiosity or hands-on work guarantees financial safety.

steps.text: Attend a paid planning demonstration after another rig crew completes a trial
Cancel the short holiday if either household rota loses paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there are two household deadlines, not just a robot date for miners. AGI in 2028 could do the invoice work, and robots around 2031 could take the rig too. We'd need employers to explain paid transitions rather than tell each family to improvise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my partner's job to go or lose most of its pay at the first stage. That would leave a mortgage we couldn't carry comfortably on my lower mine wage. The prospect wakes me up already, before I even get to the later loss of drilling work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'll ask the lender now what a temporary reduced payment would cost and put the holiday money into our reserve. I'll ask the mine about paid training to inspect drill equipment, while my partner asks for paid redeployment options. In the first year after AGI arrives we'd seek an actual replacement income before spending on any private course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed because a big part of our income looks likely to go quickly. I can make calls and examine offers, but the sums don't work just because I stay calm. I keep replaying the mortgage date at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge replacement work for either of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with our minimum monthly costs, then put each real job offer beside them. I wouldn't assume a new desk job escapes thinking AI. We'd ask what the work actually involves and whether the employer expects it still to need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the adults are checking the money and they're not responsible for fixing it. We'd stop the holiday plan without making the children feel guilty for needing school things. One lost invoice wage could put our mortgage at risk before a robot ever reaches my rig.

say: I want **paid transition plans** for both household earners, rather than advice that leaves each family to improvise.
I would explain **two deadlines**, with invoice work exposed before robots reach the drilling rig.
think: I expect **a large household loss** when AGI can replace my partner's invoice work in 2028.
I cannot comfortably cover **the mortgage** on my lower mine wage while also preparing for the later robot stage.
do: Ask the **lender** about reduced-payment costs now and move the cancelled holiday money into a reserve.
Request **paid drill-inspection training** while comparing real replacement-income offers before buying any private course.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and lose sleep because the essential household sums fail if the invoice wage disappears.
S2.quote: One lost invoice wage could put our mortgage at risk before a robot ever reaches my rig.
fieldNote: His alarm is driven by **early partner exposure**, not a mistaken claim that physical drilling disappears as soon as thinking AGI arrives.
He remains able to **compare options**, but expected substantial income loss and disrupted sleep distinguish this from ordinary unease.

steps.text: Ask the lender to explain the cost of temporary reduced payments
Move the cancelled holiday money into the household reserve
Request paid training in drill equipment inspection before buying private courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should let both employers offer something more concrete than a leaflet. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, with robots around 2034 for my physical work. I'd want preparation for the invoice job first, not a plan that starts when my rig changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra time means we could reduce dependence on the invoice wage before it disappears. I still expect that work to be heavily cut, and my drilling income later faces robots. I would be about 51 at that stage, so retirement isn't our financial plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month we'll calculate how much of the invoice wage we can save, starting with 30 a month rather than an impossible whole salary. I'll ask for a paid drill-inspection shadow shift next quarter. In the first year after AGI arrives we'd review actual household income every month and apply for inspection vacancies if the training has led somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but I can see several paydays between us and the first major loss. Five years makes building a modest reserve and trying work at different hours possible. It doesn't make either wage guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a placement workable for your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner could try a paid workplace placement while still employed, if one is offered. We'd need the hours to fit the school day or include the cost of care in the sums. I don't want to call a job a solution if the travel and care bills swallow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep the savings plan honest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd review the plan every three months instead of adding money to a spreadsheet that isn't there. If we only managed half the saving, we'd use that number. Five years gives our household time to practise living on less before a wage is taken away.

say: I want **preparation for invoice work** to start before plans for the later change to physical drilling.
I would ask **both employers** for paid practical options rather than general advice leaflets.
think: I could reduce **income dependence** over five years, although both household wages remain exposed at different stages.
I still need **work at 51**, so neither early retirement nor an imaginary large reserve is credible.
do: Begin saving **30 monthly** from household income and review what we actually managed every three months.
Request a **paid inspection shadow shift** and consider real vacancies after training, reviewing income monthly after AGI arrives.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with enough warning to practise a smaller budget and test practical work options.
S3.quote: Five years gives our household time to practise living on less before a wage is taken away.
fieldNote: He uses the longer horizon for **household adjustment**, keeping the earlier invoice exposure visible instead of focusing solely on the mine.
He checks **care and travel costs**, showing why another job title alone would not establish that the family can replace lost earnings.

steps.text: Begin saving 30 monthly and review actual progress every three months
Request a paid shadow shift inspecting drill equipment before choosing training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is long enough to plan a household change without pretending everyone has the same deadline. AGI in 2036 reaches the invoice work first, and robots around 2039 reach my rig. I'd want both workplaces to begin discussing practical routes now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 56 when robots arrive, and the children would be grown. If we use ordinary wages to reduce the mortgage, the amount we need each month could be smaller. I don't know that either of us can retire then, so I'd still test work options rather than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'll ask the lender whether small extra payments carry any fees, then choose an affordable amount only after keeping emergency cash. I'll start the inspection shadowing next quarter if a paid place is available. In the first year after thinking AI arrives we'd review our remaining debt and actual work offers, not borrow to preserve our old spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about losing income later, but the problem feels less like a trap. The children should no longer need daily care, which changes what shifts we could accept. That is breathing room, not proof the next job exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep cash instead of paying the mortgage down as fast as possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cash for a repair before sending every spare coin to the mortgage. Last month's dental bill is a useful reminder that lower debt can't buy groceries on its own. We'd ask for the fee information and then decide, not sign something at the first meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How fixed would your ten-year plan be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner we can revise the plan as the children grow and work changes. I don't want a ten-year promise that becomes an argument when life interrupts it. A smaller mortgage would help us, but a decade is not a guaranteed pension.

say: I want **both workplaces** to begin practical preparation instead of treating a decade as permission to postpone it.
I would keep the **two household stages** clear when discussing AGI and the later physical robots.
think: I expect **grown children** and a smaller mortgage could reduce what we need to earn by the robot stage.
I cannot assume **retirement at 56**, so I still need to test options for continuing paid work.
do: Ask about **mortgage fees** before making affordable extra payments while retaining cash for emergencies.
Start **paid inspection shadowing** if available and review debt and genuine offers after thinking AI arrives.
feel: I feel **anxious** about later income loss, with more breathing room as childcare demands and debt may fall.
S4.quote: A smaller mortgage would help us, but a decade is not a guaranteed pension.
fieldNote: His long-term plan retains **liquid cash**, recognising that paying debt down cannot cover an immediate repair or dental expense.
He keeps **retirement uncertain** and uses future household changes as possible flexibility rather than inventing guaranteed savings or secure work.

steps.text: Ask about mortgage fees before making affordable extra payments beyond emergency cash
Start a paid drill-inspection shadow shift if the mine offers one

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the invoice wage could go before we've changed how the household lives. We need paid routes into real work, and clear payment advice before the mortgage slips behind. Don't tell me miners are safe if the other half of the household is sitting at a screen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who watches the children while either of us trains. Two sensible job plans can still fail if both need the same afternoon. Somebody needs to put the hours on the page beside the pay.

headlineQuote: Don't tell me miners are safe if the other half of the household is sitting at a screen.
portrait: Wei is a **43-year-old drilling crew leader** with a technical diploma, two school-age children, a mortgage and less than one month saved.
His partner's **invoice work** faces thinking AI before robots reach drilling, making household exposure central to his answers.
He prefers **proven tools** and clear figures, using calendars and real offers to test plans rather than relying on reassuring titles.
Longer warnings allow **modest saving** and paid inspection trials, while childcare costs and the continued need to earn remain explicit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove the invoice wage before the household is prepared, ahead of later risks to drilling.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid work transitions**, clear mortgage advice and training hours that fit the family's childcare needs.
